evidence_quotes.quote: The material presented in this paper was gathered over a period of several months, spanning mid-2007 to early 2008. Semi-structured interviews were carried out with the residents of Sangam Vihar (our case study settlement) and private providers.

Because of their ambiguous legal status, provision of infrastructure by public utilities in such areas is limited, and the public utility for the city of Delhi – the Delhi Jal Board (DJB) – has followed an implicit policy of provisioning through bore wells and stand posts only.
The operations for piped distribution of water do not have formal recognition or legal sanction, and are effectively illegal.

In order to be eligible, settlements were required to establish registered Residents’ Societies and submit layout plans of the area, prepared through qualified professionals, to a special cell created in the Development Authority and Delhi Government, in order that settlement boundaries may be verified and development works planned in each settlement.

As a result, households’ access to the supply steadily diminishes, from a few hours each day to barely fifteen–twenty minutes a day, as the operator increases the number of households being supplied through the system.
At the time, I was paying a monthly charge of Rs 200 for a reasonable supply – I now pay Rs 600 a month, for only 1.5 hrs of supply every alternate day!

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and neighbourhood piped water supply and public bore-well/standpost access in Sangam Vihar, an unauthorised urban informal settlement in New Delhi.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain reading, the paper examines urban water governance, patronage politics, collective claim-making, and state-provider-citizen accountability relationships. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, it directly analyses concrete rule-type legal, regulatory, and institutional mechanisms governing water access: (1) settlement legal/tenure status rules under which the public utility (Delhi Jal Board, DJB) restricts unauthorised colonies to bore wells and standposts and withholds formal piped household supply until legalisation (and until formalisation of electricity supply); (2) the illegal, unsanctioned legal status of informal private piped operators (and subsequent state enforcement crackdowns on illegal tube-wells), which shapes operator risk, flat-rate tariff setting, rapid cost recovery, and arbitrary disconnections; (3) the 2008 colony regularisation eligibility and documentation requirements (registered Residents' Societies and professional layout plans); and (4) provider ownership/management and cost-recovery structures comparing unregulated informal private networks against DJB public bore-wells coupled with RWA community-managed distribution.
criterion_notes.c3: Qualitative empirical socio-legal/governance case study drawing on primary fieldwork from mid-2007 to early 2008 (semi-structured interviews with 8 resident households, 4 informal private water providers, and Residents' Welfare Association members in Blocks B and D of Sangam Vihar, plus a 2010 interview with a DJB official and comparative service-level indicators in Table 1). Qualitative socio-legal empirical studies are eligible for systematic review inclusion.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports multiple service access outcomes: exclusion from formal public utility piped water connections, household supply duration (e.g., diminishing to 15-20 minutes/day or 1.5 hours on alternate days), predictability/timing of supply, arbitrary disconnections, connection fees (Rs 500-700) and monthly user charges/affordability (INR 250-300 or Rs 600 under private operators vs. INR 50 under RWA management in Table 1), and disruption following enforcement crackdowns.
criterion_notes.c5: Clearly identifies population and units of analysis (households, informal private operators, RWAs, and settlement-level governance in Sangam Vihar, New Delhi), rule-type legal/institutional exposures, service access/reliability/affordability outcomes, and an exploratory qualitative case study design.

study_design: Exploratory qualitative case study (semi-structured interviews and comparative institutional analysis)
population_and_sample: Urban informal ('unauthorised') settlement of Sangam Vihar in southern New Delhi (0.4-0.6 million inhabitants); primary semi-structured interviews in Blocks B and D with 8 resident households, 4 informal private water providers, Residents' Welfare Association (RWA) members, and a Delhi Jal Board (DJB) official (units of analysis: settlement, provider/RWA, and household).
exposure: Unauthorised settlement legal status and Delhi Jal Board policy restricting formal piped water until regularisation; illegality/lack of regulatory sanction and enforcement crackdowns on informal private tube-well networks; 2008 regularisation eligibility and documentation requirements; and shift from unregulated private network provision to DJB bore-wells with community RWA-managed piped distribution and tariff/cost-recovery rules.
outcome: Household piped water access, supply predictability (timing), supply duration, arbitrary disconnection, connection fees, and monthly user charges/affordability (Table 1 and household interviews).
rationale: Full-text qualitative empirical case study examining how legal and institutional rules directly govern household water access in an unauthorised settlement (Sangam Vihar) in New Delhi, India. Meets all inclusion criteria under both the plain reading and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2, analysing utility legal-status restrictions on piped supply in unauthorised colonies, the illegal status and enforcement risks of informal private operators, 2008 regularisation documentation/registration rules, and provider governance/tariff structures (informal private operators vs. DJB bore-well + RWA community management) with primary interview evidence and comparative access, reliability, duration, and affordability outcomes.
